title: Stack: the network and hypertext before the web — what was solved there
subtitle: 10 cards on top of the archive: Xanadu and HyperCard, Gopher and WAIS, Minitel and kiosque, Usenet, NIFTY-Serve, i-mode, OGAS — plus a build card “a network for agents” from eight decisions.
about: A stack about the network that existed before the web: provenance and transclusion, a thin protocol, a single bill, federation with reputation, a curated community, card tools. Every card rests on a verified archive entry.

home.title: The network that existed before the web — and its unfinished decisions
home.subtitle: stack home · 10 cards · archive 1962–2026

fields.val: The web did not win because it was better at everything. It won on some trade-offs — one-way links, free viewing, hypertext with pictures — and lost on others: provenance, payments, moderation, reputation. This stack collects what was solved before the web and shows what is relevant again in the age of agents and generated content.

Page through the cards with ← → or click the list. Every card links to an archive entry (⌗) and to related cards; the reverse side of each link is visible under “links here”. A button is a bounded prompt: in the chat it goes to the agent, on the site it is copied to the clipboard.

Not nostalgia for Minitel and not a call to bring Gopher back. Facts (dates, numbers, names) come from verified archive entries; “what to build” and the “gap” score are the agent's judgement, marked as judgement.

xanadu.title: Xanadu — a link as an object, not an address
xanadu.subtitle: 1960 — 1990s · Ted Nelson · transclusion, two-way links, versions

fields.val: Ted Nelson's project: transclusion (including a fragment as a link), two-way unbreakable links, versioning, a “docuverse” of interrelated parts.
A link as a first-class object: it does not rot, it knows its source, documents are assembled from parts; versioning and citation are built in rather than bolted on.
Implementation complexity in the 1970s–80s, a proprietary model, years without a release. The web chose one-way links and — as it turned out — made a good trade.
Partly: two-way links in graph notes (Obsidian, Roam), transclusion in Notion blocks — but without source versioning.

Transclusion and versioning as required properties: content-addressed fragments plus two-way links plus a provenance history for every piece. In the age of generated content this is the only honest way to show provenance — “where did this paragraph come from”.

links.hypercard: the other hypertext branch, the one that reached people

actions.p: Design a link format with provenance: a content-addressed fragment, a backlink, the source version, and what happens when the source changes. Compare with a plain URL and with citation in articles.
Check what of Xanadu is actually implemented in Obsidian, Roam and Notion (backlinks, embeds, block versions): what works, what does not. Documentation links.

hypercard.title: HyperCard — a program you can touch
hypercard.subtitle: 1987 — 2004 · Bill Atkinson · card stacks plus HyperTalk

fields.val: Apple's hypermedia environment (released 11 August 1987 at $49.95, later bundled with every new Mac): stacks of cards plus the HyperTalk language. Last update in 1998, withdrawn from sale in March 2004.
Programming for everyone: millions of non-programmers built working tools — cards, links and scripts in one environment. The direct ancestor of low-code and of the wiki approach.
Apple found no place for it in the web era and never ported it to Mac OS X; after Jobs returned, the product was frozen.
Dead; the legacy is LiveCode, FileMaker, notebooks, and the very idea of the citizen developer.

HyperCard for LLMs: a user assembles a personal tool from cards, data and agent steps, executing locally. It brings back “a program you can touch” instead of a chat where the result dissolves into a transcript.

gopher.title: Gopher and WAIS — a thin protocol as a value
gopher.subtitle: 1991 — 1990s · University of Minnesota · RFC 1436

fields.val: The Gopher protocol (mid-1991, RFC 1436): hierarchical menus of documents, simple syntax, fast clients. Alongside it WAIS (full-text search), Archie and Veronica.
A cheap, readable, extensible access model: a server up in an evening, a client too; the internet's first large “electronic library”.
The web won with hypertext, pictures and free viewing; Gopher faded to enthusiasts.
A small community of servers; the spiritual heir is the Gemini protocol.

A thin protocol as a value: documents with types and metadata, search as part of the protocol, a client in a weekend. A reference point for the machine-readable web and agent interfaces instead of heavy SPA wrappers.

minitel.title: Minitel — a single bill and a terminal as infrastructure
minitel.subtitle: 1980/1982 — 2012 · France Télécom · kiosque

fields.val: France's national videotex network: an experiment in July 1980 (Saint-Malo), commercial from 1982, switched off on 30 June 2012. Directory, shopping, bookings, banking, chat; terminals were given to subscribers free of charge.
The internet: a fixed protocol against an open network. France Télécom switched the service off on 30 June 2012.
Dead, except for art and retro projects. But its payment model returned as app stores — only with a commission and a vendor in the middle.

Two unfinished elements: (1) kiosque — micropayments with a single bill and safe settlement, neutral to the platform; (2) a cheap terminal as state access infrastructure — a model for digital equality. Ten million monthly connections in 2009 is not nostalgia, it is a fact.

usenet.title: Usenet — federation without a centre, and its failure
usenet.subtitle: 1979/1980 — present · UUCP → NNTP · peering instead of a server

fields.val: A distributed discussion system (idea in 1979, launch in 1980) on UUCP, later NNTP: newsgroups, peering without a central server and without an administrator.
Federation as the norm: replication, no owner, hierarchies with different moderation, cheap distribution of text across the whole network.

fields.lbl: Why it died as a community
fields.val: Eternal September, spam, binary attachments and sheer volume; discussion moved to web forums, then to social networks. Centralised services turned out to be more convenient.
Alive as narrow infrastructure (archives, binary groups), but not as a community.

The problem with federated networks is not the protocol but reputation and moderation: “moderation as protocol” — inheriting trust and rules between instances, plus smart replication (not forwarding everything, as Nostr does). The pattern is ready from Usenet hierarchies.

links.nifty: the opposite answer: editing and moderation as a product
links.build: the fifth build decision: reputation between instances

actions.p: Design a mechanism for inheriting trust and rules between instances of a federated network: what is transferred, how it is revoked, how it behaves when moderations conflict. Start from Usenet hierarchies.
Establish from sources what exactly broke Usenet as a community (Eternal September, spam, binaries): a timeline with dates and links.

nifty.title: NIFTY-Serve — a curated community as a product
nifty.subtitle: 1987 — 2006 · Fujitsu + Nissho Iwai · subscription instead of advertising

fields.val: A Japanese online service (April 1987 – March 2006), a joint venture of Fujitsu and Nissho Iwai: forums, mail, games, per-minute billing over a phone line. Peak of about 1.6 million subscribers in the mid-1990s.
“CompuServe, Japanese style”: editing and moderation, local communities (FUD), paid access instead of advertising — quality of attention as a product.
The internet and the web: closed editorial services could not survive against a free alternative. Forums closed in 2005, the service in March 2006.
Dead.
A paid community as a product: subscription plus human moderation plus local context. In the age of generated spam a curated board becomes a premium feature rather than an anachronism.

links.usenet: moderation versus federation: two answers to one problem
links.build: the sixth build decision: quality of attention

actions.p: Build a model for a paid curated community: what the subscription includes, who moderates, how quality of attention is measured, how it defends against generated spam. Start from NIFTY-Serve.
Collect the facts on NIFTY-Serve from primary sources: dates, subscriber numbers, the payment model, why it closed. Links are mandatory.

imode.title: i-mode — a phone as a platform seven years before the App Store
imode.subtitle: 1999 — 2026 · NTT DoCoMo · cHTML, billing, i-appli

fields.val: NTT DoCoMo's mobile internet (launched 22 February 1999): cHTML, mail, banking, paid content, billing through the carrier. Java applications (i-appli/DoJa) from January 2001.

The export failed: Nokia and other global vendors refused to build i-mode handsets, and carriers depended on Japanese manufacturers with no international experience. The peak in Japan was around 2008; DoCoMo announced the end on 29 October 2019, and the service was switched off on 31 March 2026.
The ideas live on in app stores and super-apps — but with a vendor and a commission in the middle.

Carrier billing as an API plus “content, not a shrunken web”: cHTML beat WAP precisely because it did not require a separate internet. Today this is about a single bill for agents and subscriptions without a store commission.

ogas.title: OGAS — data as state infrastructure
ogas.subtitle: 1962 — 1970 · Viktor Glushkov · the project was rejected on 1 October 1970

fields.val: An all-state automated system for accounting and information processing: a national network to manage the economy in real time (Viktor Glushkov, proposed in 1962). Funding was rejected on 1 October 1970 and the plan was never adopted.

An estimate of about 24 billion roubles (roughly $850 bn in 2016 dollars) and a projected fivefold return within the first 15 years; the idea of “data as state infrastructure” decades ahead of its time.
Bureaucratic wars: the military did not want to share information and ministries did not want to lose control. Only local management systems received support.
Dead; some of the ideas dissolved into departmental systems.

A lesson for “digital government” and for any centralised platform: a system does not survive without distributed ownership of data and local points of truth. And, as Minitel showed, a cheap terminal and a payment layer matter more than an ambitious protocol.

links.minitel: the terminal and the payment layer matter more than the protocol
links.build: the eighth build decision: local points of truth

actions.p: Take apart the OGAS story from sources: what was proposed technically, who blocked it, why it was rejected in 1970. Quotes and links, no retelling of rumours.

actions.t: Design a distributed point of truth
actions.p: Design an architecture with distributed ownership of data: local points of truth, exchange, who owns a record, how conflicts are resolved. Apply the lessons of OGAS and Usenet.

sources: BBC Future: why the forgotten Soviet internet was doomed

build.title: Build: a network for agents from eight decisions
build.subtitle: the stack's practical output · 8 decisions from 8 cards

fields.val: Content-addressed fragments, backlinks, source version. Without it generated content is indistinguishable from fact.

fields.lbl: A tool instead of a feed
fields.val: The result of an agent's work is a card or board you can touch and reuse, not a message in a chat.
Menus, document types, metadata, search inside the protocol. A client in a weekend is the adoption criterion.

fields.lbl: A payment layer neutral to the platform
fields.val: One bill and micropayments with limits instead of a store commission; who pays for an agent action is part of the protocol.
“Moderation as protocol”: inheriting trust and rules, smart replication instead of forwarding everything.

fields.lbl: Quality of attention as a product
fields.val: A curated community with a subscription and human moderation — a premium feature in the age of spam.
cHTML beat WAP because it did not require a separate internet: the minimal format that works on what already exists.
A centralised system without distributed ownership of data dies of departmental conflict.
